newsitem.title: JAPAN: No Japan, U.S. insurance deal but talks continue.
newsitem.headline: No Japan, U.S. insurance deal but talks continue.

text.p: Japan and the United States made progress on Saturday in trying to settle their dispute over the deregulation of Tokyo's insurance market, but the talks will continue ahead of a Sunday deadline, the two sides said.

Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka and Acting United States Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky failed to reach an agreement on the dispute in their last face-to-face meeting before the self-imposed deadline.
While she was due to leave Japan later on Saturday, Barshefsky said working-level talks would continue with no extension.
"The deadline is firm and fixed and will not change," she told reporters.
The dispute has become a major irritant between the two countries, and trade experts say it could escalate into the kind of damaging trade fight that has marked U.S.-Japan relations in the past.
"We had meaningful discussions. I think we made good progress. We decided to talk on the phone later this evening," Mitsuzuka told reporters as he came out of the negotiations.
The dispute centers on U.S. charges that Japan is planning to renege on a 1994 trade agreement on the deregulation of its $400 billion insurance market.
"We managed to narrow the gap from before, but our differences over basic issues still remain," Mitsuzuka said.
Barshefsky said Japan has put forward new proposals aimed at settling the dispute.

"The Japanese government put forward new proposals which are potentially quite significant in nature. But because it's a complex area and the proposals are new, we need to evaluate them and make a determination whether the primary sector deregulation is sufficient," she said.

A key issue in the dispute is Japan's reluctance to open the main primary life and casualty insurance sector to outside companies while wanting to allow more domestic firms into a niche market where foreign firms have a current edge.
Washington has argued that the 1994 agreement calls for Tokyo to deregulate the primary sector, which is dominated by Japanese companies, before unleashing competition in the tiny specialty market.

"We have reached an agreement in principle on the insurance negotiations," Mitsuzuka said. But he declined to provide details of the agreement, saying wording of a final statement was still being discussed.

The agreement was announced after Mitsuzuka held a telephone conference call with Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky, who was at Tokyo's Narita Airport for a flight home after meeting the Japanese minister earlier in the day.
The dispute centred on U.S. charges that Japan was reneging on a 1994 trade agreement on the deregulation of its $400 billion insurance market.

Japan has been reluctant to open its main primary life and casualty insurance sector to outside companies while wanting to allow more domestic firms into a niche market where foreign firms currently have a foothold.
